intro: The three questions that keep you up at night: what this really costs per month, what data you can and can't paste in, and whether you can charge other people for it. With figures you should double-check the day you use them, and the legal side spelled out plainly.

preguntas.q: What does this really cost me per month, all in?
preguntas.a: Add up five lines and you'll have an honest number. One: the subscription you actually work with, which on entry plans runs around €23 a month. Two: pay-per-use with an API key, which only shows up if something of yours runs without you present. Three: where your website lives, free while it's just you and a handful of people you know. Four: the domain, between €5 and €15 a year. And five, the one everyone forgets and the one that weighs the most: the hours you spend maintaining it. For someone starting out, with traffic from people they know, the total usually lands around €24 a month, and twenty-three of that is the subscription you were already paying. All of these figures move every few months: check the price on the official site the day you're about to pay.
preguntas.corta: Subscription, API, hosting, domain, and your hours. Almost all of it is the subscription.

preguntas.q: Am I spending money right now without knowing it?
preguntas.a: It depends on whether you've ever entered a card. If you only type in the text box of ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, no: you're either on the free plan or paying the fixed fee, and when you go over the limit you get throttled, not overcharged. There, a surprise bill is materially impossible. If at some point you created an API key and entered a card, go into the provider's dashboard today and check three things: how much you've spent this month, whether any program of yours is currently running, and whether auto-recharge is turned on. That review takes five minutes and is the best investment of the week.
preguntas.corta: With the app, no. If you entered a card for a key, go check today.

preguntas.q: I've set up a spending alert. Am I safe now?
preguntas.a: No, and this mix-up is the most expensive one out there. An alert sends you an email saying you've spent $50 and does absolutely nothing to stop it: if you're asleep, the email arrives and the spending keeps going. A hard cap cuts off the service and returns an error, and that actually ends it. Budget alerts on some cloud platforms only notify you, and plenty of people believe otherwise until it happens to them. The brake that really works is prepaid credit with auto-recharge turned off: you put in $20, it runs out, and there's nowhere else to pull from. If your bank allows it, a virtual card with a monthly limit is the second lock, and that one doesn't depend on the platform behaving.
preguntas.corta: No. An alert is the fuel light; a cap is only having five liters.

preguntas.q: I got charged a huge spike overnight. How did that happen?
preguntas.a: It's almost always one of three things, and all three get fixed the same way. The first is auto-recharge: when you enter a card, a checkbox comes pre-checked that charges you another $10 or $20 every time your balance drops below a threshold, and a program stuck in a loop can trigger that recharge forty times in one night. The second is a leaked key: there are bots scanning the internet for those strings of text, and if yours shows up somewhere public, it gets used within minutes. The third is an agent you gave permission to retry when something fails, and it retries eight thousand times. The fix for all three isn't watching more closely: it's making sure there's no available money to spend.
preguntas.corta: Auto-recharge, a leaked key, or a loop. Remove the available money.

preguntas.q: Why does a long chat cost more than a short one?
preguntas.a: Because the AI has no memory and has to be reminded of everything every time. Every message you write resends the entire conversation from the start, so your fortieth message is dragging along the previous thirty-nine. A long conversation doesn't cost forty times the first question, it costs far more than that. If you pay per use, you feel it in dollars; if you pay a subscription, you feel it in running out of quota sooner once you've spent three hours in the same thread. That's why the single most effective savings trick isn't writing less: it's opening a new conversation every time you switch topics.
preguntas.corta: Because it resends the whole thread each time. Start a new chat when you switch topics.

preguntas.q: Am I overpaying by using the most powerful model?
preguntas.a: Probably, yes. The price difference between the large model and the small one is roughly a hundred times, and for half of all tasks the small one does exactly the same job. Classifying an email, sorting data, pulling a summary, or tagging a message doesn't need the expensive model. The large one earns its keep when you actually need to reason through a problem with many moving parts. The way to decide isn't by gut feeling: run the same task through both on ten cases of your own, compare the results, and stick with the cheap one if you don't see a difference. Per-use prices are quoted per million tokens and change often, so check the exact figure on the official site that day.
preguntas.corta: Probably. For classifying and summarizing, the small model does just as well.

preguntas.q: Can I paste my clients' data into ChatGPT?
preguntas.a: You can, with conditions, and it's not a plain yes. The moment you handle personal data (a name, an email, a phone number, anything that identifies someone) you're inside GDPR and your country's data protection law, and that doesn't depend on how big your business is. Three bare minimums: use a paid or business account where you can check what they do with your data, strip out anything the AI doesn't need for the task before pasting it, and inform the person with a simple line saying you use automated systems and that a person reviews the output. And a common-sense rule: if you'd be embarrassed for that text to end up in someone else's hands, don't paste it. For a project with sensitive data or for a client, have someone qualified review it.
preguntas.corta: With conditions. Strip what's unneeded, inform people, and use a paid account.

preguntas.q: What should I never paste in?
preguntas.a: There's a short list that isn't negotiable. ID or passport numbers, bank account and card numbers, passwords and API keys. Health, ideology, religion, union membership, or sexual orientation data. Anything about a minor. A client's entire contracts, payslips, or files when all you need is a small part of them. And documentation covered by a confidentiality agreement you've signed. Most of that isn't even needed for the task: if you want it to draft a reply, it doesn't need anyone's ID number. Strip those fields out before sending the text, and if health data or data about minors comes up, stop and consult someone. That's not something a line in a disclaimer fixes.
preguntas.corta: IDs, accounts, health, minors, whole contracts, and keys. None of that is needed.

preguntas.q: Does the AI train on what I write?
preguntas.a: It depends on the plan and the provider, and it changes over time, so the right answer is for you to check it yourself. Generally, free accounts tend to be the most permissive and business or API accounts the most restrictive, but don't assume anything. What you can do today: go into the privacy settings of whatever tool you use, find the checkbox about improving the model with your conversations, and set it how you want. Even with it turned off, your conversations stay stored for a while on their servers for security and support purposes. Training and storage are two different things, and it's worth not mixing them up when you explain this to a client.
preguntas.corta: It depends on the plan. Check the box in settings, don't assume.

preguntas.q: I'm self-employed. What does GDPR require of me if I start using AI to work?
preguntas.a: Four concrete things, and none of them requires a degree. One: a record of processing activities. If the processing isn't occasional (and a daily automated flow isn't), you need to keep one even if you're a one-person operation. It's a document where you note what data you handle, for what purpose, how long you keep it, and who accesses it. Two: the model provider is a data processor, so you need a contract with them; the big providers offer one already signed within their terms, you just accept and keep it. Three: inform the person, with a line in the form or in your email signature. And four: decide how long you keep things and delete them when it's time. This is practical guidance, not legal advice: if the project handles sensitive data or is for a client, have someone qualified review it.
preguntas.corta: A processing record, a contract with the provider, informing people, and deleting on schedule.

preguntas.q: The provider processes data in the United States. Is that a problem?
preguntas.a: It's not a closed door, but it is something you need to know and note down. When data leaves the European Union, the transfer has to rest on something: whichever adequacy framework is in force at that moment, or the standard contractual clauses the provider includes in its terms. What you're really being asked to do is this: check where the provider says it processes data, confirm what legal basis it relies on, and write down both, with the date you checked. Several providers let you choose a processing region on business plans, and if you can choose Europe, do. This area shifts with court rulings, so for a client it's worth having someone qualified confirm it.
preguntas.corta: It doesn't block anything, but note what basis you're relying on and the date you checked.

preguntas.q: Can the AI decide about a person on its own? Like denying an application?
preguntas.a: That's where you need to stop. GDPR's Article 22 restricts decisions made solely by a machine when they have legal effects on someone or similarly affect them: denying credit, ruling out a candidate, canceling a service. The practical fix is that the AI proposes and a person decides. And that human review has to be real: someone who reads, who can change the proposal, and who sometimes does. If it's a hundred approvals in a row with zero corrections and two seconds per case, that's not review, that's a button. Keep a record of who approved what and when, because the day someone files a complaint, that log is the only thing you have.
preguntas.corta: Not on its own. The AI proposes, a person decides — for real, and on record.

preguntas.q: How do I know if the AI made something up?
preguntas.a: First, drop the instinct that betrays you: what it makes up doesn't come out looking like a fabrication, it comes out looking as convincing as possible. It has learned the shape of true things better than the true things themselves, so a fake phone number carries the right area code and a fake citation matches the format to the letter. The question that separates safe from dangerous is a single one: can I judge this just by reading it, or would I have to go check it somewhere else? The tone of an email, the structure of a text, or a summary of a document you pasted in yourself — you judge those by reading them. Names, figures, dates, prices, phone numbers, links, and legal citations need to be checked against the original source. Those are facts, and facts always get verified.
preguntas.corta: If you'd need to go check it elsewhere, it's a fact. And facts get checked.

preguntas.q: I asked it if it was sure and it said yes. Does that count?
preguntas.a: It counts for nothing, and it's the worst question you can ask it. There's no mechanism in there that knows whether it got it right: what's in there is a machine calculating what text fits under yours, and what usually fits under "are you sure?" is an apology and a new version, just as made up, or worse. Asking that doesn't verify anything, it just gives you a second answer with the same confidence. What actually works is asking for the source and opening it yourself, turning on web search and clicking the links, or pasting in the real document and telling it to stick to it. One warning: with search turned on, the fabrication comes disguised as a source, which is worse, because the link makes you relax.
preguntas.corta: No. Asking "are you sure?" verifies nothing. Ask for the source and open it yourself.

preguntas.q: It cited a legal statute for me. Can I trust it?
preguntas.a: Law names, article numbers, and court rulings sit at the very top of the risk list, and there the error isn't an anecdote. There are famous cases of lawyers filing court briefs citing rulings that didn't exist: real companies, real courts, a citation format identical to the genuine article. When the judge asked for the copies, the AI generated them whole. So with legal matters the rule is strict: the text of the law gets opened at the official source and read there. Check your country's official gazette and the data protection authority's website, which also publishes plain-language guides for small businesses. And if a decision affecting someone hinges on that article, don't leave it in your hands or the AI's: have someone qualified review it.
preguntas.corta: No. Laws and rulings get opened at the official source. It's where fabrication is worst.

preguntas.q: How do I stop the AI from promising a client something that isn't true?
preguntas.a: With three things at once, and all three are needed. One: put the closed list of true facts, the real prices and deadlines, inside the brief, and tell it to use only those. Two: the rule of writing "MISSING DATA" instead of filling in the gap, because its instinct is always to fill it in. And three: a person approves before anything goes out. With only the first and second, it'll fail you someday; with only the third, you'll review poorly out of fatigue. And keep what the AI proposed alongside what actually went out: comparing the two tells you exactly where your brief falls short, and that's how you improve it with data instead of opinions.
preguntas.corta: True facts in the brief, the MISSING DATA rule, and a person who approves.

preguntas.q: Can I charge other people for doing this?
preguntas.a: Yes, and no certification is required to stop you. What does apply are the normal obligations of anyone billing clients: being registered with the tax authorities if this stops being occasional, issuing invoices with tax, and filing your returns. On top of that, if you're going to touch data belonging to your client's clients, you become a data processor for them and you both need a written contract saying so. Also put in writing what you deliver, what you don't, and what happens when something fails. Check the tax side with your accountant, since it depends on your situation, and for a contract involving data, have someone qualified review it.
preguntas.corta: Yes. Registration, invoices, and a written contract if you touch their clients' data.

preguntas.q: And how much do I charge? I have no idea where to start.
preguntas.a: Don't charge by the hour, charge by the deliverable, and start by selling a standalone diagnostic: map the process, measure volume and time, and put in writing what can be automated and what can't, without building anything. That's worth $400-900 on its own, even if the client doesn't move forward. Building a minimal setup (a channel, classification, a spreadsheet, and alerts) runs $1,500-3,000, and a fuller one with several channels and an approval step runs $3,500-8,000. Always add maintenance, $150-500 a month, because this breaks on its own: an API changes, a permission expires, a new kind of case shows up. These are rough market ranges for small projects: adjust them to your area, your experience, and how messy the client's data is.
preguntas.corta: By deliverable, not by hour. Start by selling the standalone diagnostic.

preguntas.q: The client asks where their data ends up and what happens if the AI gets it wrong. What do I tell them?
preguntas.a: Tell them the truth, with names and numbers, because that's the only thing that survives a meeting. About data: which provider holds it, under what contract, in what region it's processed, what fields you strip before sending, and the date you last checked all that. About errors: that it does get things wrong, that you've measured it against a batch of hand-reviewed cases, and that's exactly why the system proposes but doesn't send without a person approving. Add how it can be stopped in two minutes and how you fall back to the manual process, and rehearse that in front of them. Nobody's going to buy "this never fails," and it also isn't true.
preguntas.corta: The truth, with names and numbers: where data lives, what you strip, who approves.
